intro: John Michel plays the Prélude from Bach’s Cello Suite No. 1, BWV 1007. The single line moves through broken chords and then scales before the final G-major chord.

sections.label: A · G major broken chords
sections.mNote: Broken chords above a moving bass line

sections.label: B · Scales after the held D
sections.mNote: The cello continues in scales after the fermata.

sections.label: Coda · Chromatic climb above D
sections.mNote: The upper notes rise towards the final G-major chord.

cues.title: Opening arpeggio, bars 1–4
cues.text: The cello plays the notes G, D and B one at a time. The low G returns throughout bars 1–4 while the bow moves through the notes above it. There is no accompaniment, so the cello plays both the bass and the upper line.
cues.evidence: Schirmer score (1916), Prelude, bars 1–4, in the Mutopia edition: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=517.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Anna Magdalena Bach’s copy
cues.text: Bach’s own manuscript of the cello suites is lost. They survive in copies, one of them made by his wife, Anna Magdalena. Her slurs are inconsistent, so cellists must choose their own bowings for these broken chords.
cues.evidence: No autograph of the Cello Suites survives; Anna Magdalena Bach’s copy and its slurring are discussed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cello_Suites_(Bach) (Manuscript section) and in the Netherlands Bach Society’s notes on BWV 1007, https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-1007.

cues.title: Fermata on D, bar 22
cues.text: A rising arpeggio reaches D and stops on a fermata. The cello then continues in freer semiquaver scales, leaving the repeated pattern of the opening. D belongs to the dominant of G.
cues.evidence: Schirmer score (1916), Prelude, bar 22 and following: fermata on D followed by freer semiquaver figuration. Mutopia edition, music ID 517.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Pedal D under a chromatic ascent
cues.text: A repeated D alternates with a line rising by semitones, and the cello keeps returning to the D as the upper notes climb past it. One last round of broken chords leads to a full G-major chord.
cues.evidence: Schirmer score (1916), Prelude, bars 37–42: chromatic ascent alternating with D, then broken chords and the final G-major chord. Mutopia edition, music ID 517.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: Fermata on D, then a rising scale
transitions.to: B · Scales after the held D
transitions.how: In bar 22 the cello climbs to a D marked with a fermata. After the pause, semiquavers run up the scale and spread across a wider range. The bass and upper notes are still played by a single bow. D is the dominant of G, and the harmony does not yet resolve to the tonic.
transitions.evidence: Schirmer score (1916), Prelude, bar 22 and following; Mutopia edition, music ID 517.

transitions.title: Dominant pedal on D, rising line
transitions.from: B · Scales after the held D
transitions.how: The cello alternates D with a rising chromatic line. The repeated D is a dominant pedal, and the upper notes rise above it. Broken chords then lead through the final cadence to G major, which is held under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Schirmer score (1916), Prelude, bars 37–42; Mutopia edition, music ID 517.

composer.epithet: Composer who supplied music for Leipzig’s churches for twenty-seven years and wrote a large body of keyboard music.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, were found in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. In his cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, one voice sings the psalmist’s plea while another sings a hymn in long notes above it.
